The returned table has one row per selected edge only: edge 2 from node 2 to 3, and edge 6 from node 4 to 5." width="100%"} Exports the currently selected edges, one row per edge, as a Polars DataFrame. It is the selection-scoped version of `get_edge_df()`: narrow the edges down with one of the `select_edges...` methods (or an edge traversal), then use Polars to filter, aggregate, join, or write the result to disk. The graph and the selection are not modified. Use this when: - inspecting the weights or relationship types of a subset of edges - computing statistics (e.g., mean weight) for edges matching some condition - exporting part of an edge list for reporting or for building another graph Sources and targets are given as integer node IDs; join with `get_node_df()` (or use `get_label_from_id()`) to recover labels. Attribute columns are built only from the selected edges, so an attribute present elsewhere in the graph but not on any selected edge will not appear. A `weight` column is included only if at least one selected edge is weighted. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [pl.DataFrame]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : DataFrame with edges sorted by id, containing: - column 1: `id` (i64, mandatory) - column 2: `source` (i64, mandatory) - column 3: `target` (i64, mandatory) - column 4: `rel` (str, mandatory, `None` if not set) - columns 5-N: other attributes, including `weight` when present (alphabetically sorted, `None` where an edge lacks the attribute) If no edges are selected, the DataFrame has no rows and just the `id`, `source`, `target` and `rel` columns (and `weight` on a weighted graph). ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Same schema as `get_edge_df()` (`id`, `source`, `target`, `rel` first, then other attributes in alphabetical order, sorted by `id`), but scoped to the current edge selection. An empty selection returns an empty DataFrame, so one of the `select_edges...` methods needs to run first. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Selecting only the "friend" edges before exporting means the DataFrame contains just that subset, edges `1` and `3`: ::: {#ff0bbdf7 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) .add_edges( [ ("A", "B", 1.5, {"rel": "friend"}), ("B", "C", 0.5, {"rel": "colleague"}), ("C", "D", 2.0, {"rel": "friend"}), ] ) .select_edges(lambda e: e.attributes and e.attributes.get("rel") == "friend") ) graph.get_edge_df_ws() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}

The mean weight of the selected friend edges is `(1.5 + 2.0) / 2`: ::: {#0f76bb79 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.get_edge_df_ws()["weight"].mean() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 1.75 ``` ::: ::: Edges can also be selected by ID. Here the first three edges of a 10-node path are exported; the `weight` column is absent because none of them is weighted: ::: {#ac5675fc .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph().add_path_graph(10) edge_ids = list(graph.get_edge_ids())[:3] graph.select_edges_by_id(edge_ids) graph.get_edge_df_ws() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
